attributes.title: Level 2

subgroups.name: build 1

steps.hints: ❓ Are the asteroid sprite’s blocks in the [on game update every ms] loop with sprite kind Enemy?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:

Ask the ninja:

❓Did you drag the asteroid’s [set sprite position to] block below its [set sprite to] block?

❓ What do you notice about the [on game update every ms] loop? What do you think it will allow you to do?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 The [on game update every ms] adds a loop into the code. This means that the actions within the container block will repeat continuously, every 500 ms (0.5 seconds) while the game is played.
steps.instructions:
Asteroids are falling from the sky!


Open the Game code block menu then drag out an [on game update every ms] container block. 


The [on game update every ms] container block is a loop. This means that the actions within the container block will repeat continuously while the game is played.  


Drag the asteroid sprite’s [set sprite to] and [set sprite position to] blocks out of the [on start] container block into the [on game update every ms] loop. Update the asteroid sprite’s sprite kind to Enemy.


Click ▶ to see the Player and Enemy sprites appear on screen!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you change the sprite name in [set sprite velocity to] to the Enemy sprite you want to move?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:

﻿


Ask the ninja:

❓ What do you already know about a sprite’s velocity?

❓When you click ▶, what do you notice about the asteroid’s direction and speed?

❓What does the [on game update every ms] loop block do? 


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Velocity may be a new term for a ninja. Guide the ninja to think about the block as the speed that the sprite moves in a certain direction, which is determined by the number of pixels left/right and up/down it is moving by.
steps.instructions:
The Enemy sprites aren’t moving yet.


Open the Sprites code block menu then drag out a [set sprite velocity to] block into the [on game update every ms] loop. Velocity is the speed of something moving in a certain direction.


Change the sprite name in the [set sprite velocity to] block, but don’t change the vx or vy values.


Click ▶ to see many Enemy sprites come down from the top of the screen.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you drag a [pick random] block in the x  parameter bubble of the Enemy’s [set position to] block and change the values?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:


Ask the ninja:

❓ How does the [pick random] block affect where the asteroid falls from?

❓ What if you wanted to make the asteroids fall randomly from only the left or right side of the screen? How would you change the x values?

❓ Why is it helpful to keep the y value at 0? How does this change where the asteroid falls from?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡Randomness can introduce a fun element of surprise into a ninja’s project. Guide the ninja to tinker with x values within the [pick random] bubble to explore its effects.

💡Guide the ninja to notice that the two parameters indicate a range of possible numbers from a lesser valued number to a greater valued number.
steps.instructions:
Code each new Enemy sprite to start in a random position!


Open the Math code block menu, then drag out a [pick random] value block and insert it into the x value parameter for the [set sprite position to] block.


Change the numbers to 0 and 160 so the Enemy sprites will start somewhere between the far left and far right sides of the screen.


Click ▶ to see the Enemy sprites start in different locations as they come down from the top.

steps.hints: ❓ What sprite name did you select to bounce on the wall?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:


Ask the ninja:

❓ How does the [set sprite bounce on wall] block change the asteroid’s movement? Why does it make the game more fun to play?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Remind the ninja that they need to set the toggle to “on,” to ensure that the asteroid bounces when it hits the wall.

💡 Help the ninja notice the connection between the [set sprite bounce on wall] and the [set sprite stay in screen] blocks. Prompt the ninja to identify the similarities and reflect on why they might use one block instead of the other.
steps.instructions:
Make the game more exciting by setting the Enemy sprites to bounce on the screen walls!


Open the Sprites code block menu then drag out a [set sprite bounce on wall] block into the [on game update every ms] loop.


Click ▶ to see the screen fill with Enemy sprites!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you change the value in the [on game update every ms] loop to a number bigger than 500 ms?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:


Ask the ninja:

❓ Did you tinker with the time length parameter in the the [on game update every ms] loop? 

❓What did you observe about the number of asteroids on the screen as you tried out different lengths of time?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Help the ninja notice that the time parameter in the [on game update every ms] loop is presented in milliseconds (ms). This means that if they’d like something to repeat continuously every 1 second, it will show up as 1000 ms.
steps.instructions:
Too many Enemy sprites are on the screen!


Change the parameter in the [on game update every ms] loop to change how often the code inside the loop runs. 


Click ▶ to see how changing the parameter changes the number of Enemy sprites on the screen.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you set vy to 0  in the Player sprite’s [move sprite with buttons] block?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:

Ask the ninja:

❓ Why might you want the Player sprite to only move left and right? 

❓ If you wanted the Player sprite to only move up and down, what would you change?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Guide the ninja to notice that the order of the code blocks matters. Any block that refers to a sprite needs to come after its [set sprite to] block.
steps.instructions:
Code the Player sprite to move left and right, and stay in screen.


On the [move sprite with buttons] block, click + then change vy to 0 so the sprite can only move left and right. Set the Player sprite to stay in screen.


Click ▶ to move your Player sprite left and right to avoid the Enemy sprites!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you change the sprite kind parameters so the [on sprite overlaps sprite] checks if the Player overlaps the Enemy, and then destroys the otherSprite?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:

﻿

Ask the ninja:❓ Did you test out different effects and sounds, and select ones that you like?❓What else could happen when the Player sprite overlaps with the Enemy sprite?

Sensei Pro Tip:💡 The sprite kind information will be used instead of the sprite names in the [on sprite overlaps sprite] container block. Instead of specifying one sprite, the overlap code will affect all sprites of a certain kind.💡 Remind the ninja that the time parameter is presented in milliseconds (ms) and that 1000 ms is equal to 1 second.
steps.instructions:
Code something to happen when the Player sprite overlaps one of the Enemy sprites.


Open the Sprites code block menu then drag out an [on sprite overlaps sprite] container block. 


Change the (otherSprite) kind to Enemy, then destroy the (otherSprite) and play a sound when the Player and Enemy sprites overlap. Click + on the [destroy sprite] block to change the effect parameter.  Notice how using the [otherSprite] bubble allows only the Enemy sprite overlapped to be destroyed, rather than specifying the specific sprite name.


Click ▶ to see what happens when the Enemy sprites touch the Player sprite.

steps.hints: ❓ Where did you drag the [set life to] block? Did you [change life by] -1 in the [on sprite overlaps sprite]?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:

Ask the ninja:❓ Did you test out a different number of lives in the [set life to] block? How might that change a player’s experience of this game?❓ What else might you add to cause the Player sprite to lose or gain a life?

Sensei Pro Tip:💡 Guide the ninja to try out different parameters for the life variable. Just like with speed and other parameters, there is no perfect number of lives.
steps.instructions:
Track the Player sprite’s lives.


Drag out a [set life to] block into the [on start] container block to set the life variable. 


Drag out a [change life by] block into the [on sprite overlaps sprite] container block to change the life variable when the Player and Enemy sprites overlap.


Click ▶ to see the Player sprite’s lives go down when an Enemy sprite overlaps with it.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you set the toggle to “WIN” in the [on countdown end] block?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:



Ask the ninja:❓ What else could happen when the countdown ends?

Sensei Pro Tip:💡Guide ninjas to try out different amounts of time to make the game exciting but not too short.
steps.instructions:
The Player sprite should win if it avoids the Enemy sprites until the time runs out.


Drag out a [start countdown] block into the [on start] container block to set the countdown timer variable.


Drag out an [on countdown end] container block with a [game over] block inside to control what happens when the timer runs out.


Click ▶ to see the Player sprite win the game if it avoids the Enemy sprites while the timer is running.

steps.hints: ❓ Which code blocks would you use to add a splash screen or dialog box to your game?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:


Ask the ninja:

❓What directions will help people understand how your project works?

❓ How might you customize what the dialog frame and text color look like?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡Guide ninjas to note that while these customizing blocks are open ended and not required for the game to “work”, they really improve the Player’s experience playing a game, either by giving context to what the Player should do or not do, or to provide a more fun experience overall. They also allow the Ninja to add their personal touch and express themselves through small details present in the game.
steps.instructions:
Customize this game by adding directions at the beginning with a splash screen or dialog boxes.


Click ▶ to see the completed game project!

subgroups.title: Avoid the Asteroids!
subgroups.introduction: Create a game with lots of Enemy sprites that keep appearing with the help of a loop! Win by staying away from the Enemy sprites until the timer runs out.

validationItems.text: Use a Game Update loop to create Enemy sprites
Start the Enemy sprite in a random position
Set the Enemy sprite to bounce when it hits a wall
Move the Player left and right with the direction buttons and set the Player sprite to stay in screen.
Destroy the Enemy sprite with an effect when it overlaps the Player sprite
Set the life variable at the beginning of the game  and set it to decrease when the Player and Enemy sprites overlap
Use a countdown timer, and set the player to win the game when it reaches 0.
Add dialog boxes or a splash screen with game directions

attributes.description: You’ve reached Level 2 of Yellow Belt! In this level, you’ll learn about loops, which are chunks of code that repeat a sequence of instructions. Here are the achievements you’ll unlock in Level 2:

badges.title: Around and Around
badges.description: Use loops to repeat code in a project.

badges.title: The Times, They Are A-Changin’
badges.description: Use a game update loop to repeat actions in a project.

badges.title: Bouncing off the Walls
badges.description: Set a sprite to bounce on walls in a project.

badges.title: Pew Pew
badges.description: Launch a projectile from a specific sprite.

badges.title: Button Masher
badges.description: Use an event triggered by the A button in a project.

badges.title: I Like to Move It Move It
badges.description: Use velocity to make a sprite move on its own.
